#55835. Latest Update: What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Latest Update: What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think.
  • Not all electronic cords look the same.
  • Sources indicate that those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Sources indicate that those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

Recent findings suggest that the holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

Industry observers note that “TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”.

According to recent reports, manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

It has been revealed that the holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

Good ice can make an ordinary drink feel special, and the GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro lets you enjoy that feeling of luxury right at home. Designed to start producing ice in mere minutes and to fill its 3.5-pound bucket in about an hour and a half, it churns out small, consistently sized nuggets that scoop easily and chill drinks rapidly. But weighing a little over 40 pounds, it’s not a countertop appliance you want to move around—and it’s not cheap either. Which begs the question: Is the Nugget Ice Maker Pro worth the space and investment? I tested it to find out.

Sources indicate that the Nugget Ice Maker Pro started producing ice within minutes of setup, and filling the entire 3.5-pound bucket took less than 90 minutes. If you emptied it after each fill, that would mean you could make up to 60 pounds of ice in about 24 hours. While we have no need for that much ice, my family of three (and often more with my daughter’s friends around) never encountered an empty bin during our 2 weeks of testing. We used it for everything from filling our massive water bottles and making super-cold fruit smoothies to hosting a house full of teenagers on Halloween.

But that impressive quantity isn’t this machine’s best feature—the ice it makes is. Popularized by drive-thru restaurants like Sonic, nugget ice has a somewhat soft, air-pocketed texture that soaks up your drink’s flavor while also being easy to chew. That crunchable quality makes it as perfect for iced coffee, lemonade, and specialty cocktails as it is for blending smooth in a shake.

When we first set up the GoveeLife, we put it in our kitchen, since that seemed logical. But at 21.3 inches deep by 13.98 inches wide by 17.02 inches high, it was simply too big for our very small kitchen. Luckily, moving it to the garage was incredibly easy, and because the 4.9-liter water reservoir is detachable, we just carry that part inside when it’s time to refill.

According to recent reports, scooping from the Ice Maker Pro is equally straightforward. The scoop attaches magnetically to the side, so it’s never buried in the ice bin or accidentally set down in some odd place. And there’s a drawer catch so that you don’t pull too hard and end up with ice all over your floor. We went the set-it-and-forget-it route of simply programming it to make new ice any time we scooped some out, but you can also control production through the Govee app, Alexa, or Google Home. In terms of maintenance, the 10-minute quick-cleaning mode handles most of the work, but you’ll also want to run the 30-minute deep descaling mode and hand-wash the removable parts occasionally.

According to recent reports, at roughly 43 pounds and almost $500, the GoveeLife Ice Maker isn’t small, and it isn’t cheap. But if you have the space and love nugget ice, its sleek finish, customizable RGB lighting, and quality cubes will be right at home in your kitchen or home bar. Regardless of location, however, the appeal is the same: quick production, consistent nuggets, and enough capacity to handle everyday drinks and entertainment. We love ours, and it’s officially staying put.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A.
  • Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A.
  • Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):.

In "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again.".

Although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.

It is not for me at my time of life to learn a upcoming language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

According to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

But lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times.

Industry observers note that he labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:.

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

From oil-filled radiators to faux fireplaces and more, there is no shortage of options when it comes to space heaters for basements. Choosing the right one depends on factors, including the size of the space, desired temperature range, and budget. An electric space heater can help keep the pipes from freezing or create a cozy living space. Our product reviews team researched and tested 13 space heaters that meet a variety of heating needs.

In a recent development, the Dr. Infrared DR-968 was our favorite. Its strong heat output, easy-to-use controls, and moderate price point made it a great option for a variety of heating needs. The wood casing was more attractive than other designs we tested, too, but it was bigger and heavier than most. Other heaters were more compact and lighter weight, making them easier to transport and better suited for smaller spaces.

Industry observers note that regardless of the size or look of your basement space, if it needs supplemental heating, be sure to read the individual reviews for notes on each heater we tested. This list includes some of the best space heaters for basements of all types.

Ahead, we offer our hands-on reviews to help you find a good space heater for basement heating. Based on more than 2 weeks of testing, we feel that any one of these options is a good choice depending on specific requirements.

For a good all-purpose space heater, it’s hard to beat the Dr. Infrared DR-968 Portable Space Heater. It utilizes what the manufacturer describes as “advanced dual-heating technology,” which combines infrared tubes with ceramic elements to quickly warm large basements. In our tests, it was easy to control, operated quietly, and heated large areas efficiently.

The digital thermostat allows precise temperature settings between 50 and 85 degrees Fareinheit. It did a great job keeping our test area comfortable without noticeable temperature dips or spikes, kicking on and off very quietly. Settings are 1,500 watts (W) for high, 1,000W for low, and eco mode for maximum energy efficiency. A quiet 39-decibel fan helps push heat around the room. We also appreciated the 12-hour timer function, and that all settings can be managed via the handheld remote control.

Recent findings suggest that we especially liked the wood exterior, which gave it an appearance more like furniture and less like an appliance. The exterior did get warm but not hot, so this Dr. Infrared space heater is safe for use around children and animals. There is overheating and tip-over protection, and the unit is UL listed. At 24 pounds, it isn’t the lightest model, and while it does have casters, they are plastic rather than metal.

What our tester says: “The Dr. Infrared DR968 earned its place at the top of our guide with fast, quiet heating, intuitive controls, and looks that blend nicely with living room furniture. The build quality was top-notch, too. This was the one we kept going back to after testing was over.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Sources indicate that get the Dr. Infrared space heater for basements at Amazon or The Home Depot.

If affordability tops your list of shopping priorities, consider the Comfort Zone Convection Baseboard Heater. It was the lowest-priced model we tested, but it heated our space well. This model features a low-profile design that, at 29 inches wide, fits perfectly beneath a cold window, where its radiant heat can passively offset any draft. This unit offers a choice of 750W or 1,500W output and an adjustable thermostat. It produces gentle heat for modest-sized spaces.

The controls for the thermostat and power level are simple knobs, making the Comfort Zone baseboard heater one of the easiest units to operate. However, there is no economy mode, timer, or circulating fan. It is ETL listed with a cool-touch body and has both overheating and tip-over protection. It raised the temperature in our test space 5 degrees in less than 30 minutes, and it did a good job of maintaining a consistent temperature. This is a basic, low-wattage space heater​ without many extra features, but the price is very competitive.

What our tester notes: “I was surprised how well this small space heater worked in our test area. I set it up below a drafty basement window, and when the heat combined with the cold draft, we noticed an immediate improvement. Fixing the draft with weather stripping will be more effective, but it was nice to see what this heater can do, even without a fan.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Comfort Zone space heater for basements at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

Industry observers note that we value ceramic space heaters for their quick, portable, energy-efficient heating ability, and because they are more affordable than other options. The compact H3 ceramic space heater from Dreo proved to be one of our favorites of the test group, earning high scores in every category. It weighs under 5 pounds and stands just under 16 inches tall, yet it had no problem heating our 200-square-foot space within 20 minutes. It comes with a variety of handy features, including four heat settings, oscillating motion, a programmable thermostat, and a fan-only option.

We were impressed by the Dreo H3’s speed and range of heating. The warmth was palpable almost immediately after turning it on, and it filled the space rapidly without drying the air like other heaters. As an added bonus, it’s available in two colorways, black and gold or black and silver, to coordinate with different home decor.

Get the Dreo space heater at Amazon or Dreo.

Those looking for the most energy-efficient space heater should consider a micathermic model. Micathermic space heaters combine infrared heating with convection for maximum heating efficiency. The De’Longhi HMP1500 raised the temperature in our 200-square-foot space by 5 degrees in just 20 minutes. The flat panel puts out radiant heat at the front of the heater while the sides and back of the unit stay cool. This space-saving unit offers the flexibility to be either wall-mounted or freestanding and includes casters.

Setting up the unit was a cinch. The casters simply twisted into the base by hand. No tools were necessary. We did not attempt the wall-mount, as drywall anchors were not included with the kit. The only controls were two dials on the side of the heater: one to adjust the heat level, the other for the fan speed. Once the room was heated, this unit maintained a fairly steady temperature. The front panel does get hot to the touch, so we don’t recommend it for families with small children, unless extra precautions are taken.

Get the De’Longhi space heater for basements at De’Longhi.

For year-round comfort, it’s tough to beat the 2-in-1 Shark TurboBlade Fan Heater. It heats and cools with independently controllable heating and fan functions, and features Thermo IQ smart temperature control to maintain your ideal temperature. This unit also includes a remote control with magnetic docking.

The TurboBlade was one of the most adjustable heaters we tested. In addition to offering three heat settings and ten fan speeds, it can be configured as a 180-degree oscillating tower with vertical output, or the head can pivot to deliver wide horizontal airflow. Bladeless airflow ensures a steady, gentle breeze.

The TurboBlade Fan Heater was easy to set up and adjust. It operated with almost no noise, heated our 200-square-foot space quickly and evenly, and maintained a very consistent temperature. Of all the space heaters we tested that were equipped with fans, this one was the quietest. We really liked the slim profile, too. In the vertical position, it was easy to store when not in use, making it a good portable heater for basement​ spaces.

Space heaters need not be big, bulky, and unattractive. This one from Lasko’s designer series features smooth contours and an attractive base, giving it the appearance of a piece of pottery or a sculpture rather than a simple appliance. It looks great, and it heats rooms up to 150 square feet, with a smooth oscillating motion that creates a thorough warming effect. It also includes a remote control.

Recent findings suggest that in our tests, this unit outperformed our expectations. Testing it in a 200-square-foot space, we anticipated modest results. Were we wrong. We were impressed with its strong heat output and even heating ability. We liked having the option to choose a precise temperature setting (in 5-degree increments). We also appreciated that it included an optional auto-shutoff timer with 1, 2, and 4-hour settings, although we didn’t leave it on while we were away.

The only thing we didn’t love about this heater was that it completely shuts off when the room reaches the target temperature. It is not designed to kick back on to maintain the temperature. Instead, we had to turn it back on each time the temperature dropped. Thanks to the remote, we didn’t have to get up to do so.

Get the Lasko space heater for basements at Walmart.

Sources indicate that while basement space heaters are not necessarily known for their looks, this Duraflame electric faux woodstove is both stylish and heat efficient. The steel and glass housing, available in 5 color options, mimics the look of a traditional woodstove. Adjustable 3-D flame effects add a realistic visual element, with glowing logs and flickering flames that are controlled independently of the heating element. This unit also includes a remote control.

The Duraflame space heater warmed our 200-square-foot test area by 7 degrees in just 15 minutes. It is designed for use in areas up to 1,000 square feet. With ample heat output and a strong circulation fan to help spread the warmth throughout the area, we believe it could easily support the larger space.

Industry observers note that this unit has a single power setting for heat, with a digital thermostat to turn it on and off as needed. It is also equipped with an 8-hour timer. The onboard controls and digital display are neatly hidden behind the door panel. The Duraflame space heater costs a bit more than others we tested, but its appearance and strong heating ability justify the price.

Get the Duraflame space heater for basements at Amazon, Walmart, or Wayfair.

We researched dozens of space heaters from the most popular brands before choosing our top seven prospects for testing. We wanted to find out if more expensive options really worked better, or if the cheaper models offered safe and dependable, budget-friendly heating solutions. Recent findings suggest that tesla prepares to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk indicates Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images.

According to recent reports, in a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Recent findings suggest that current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

Tesla hasn’t said which customers will receive their trucks or how it prepares to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The tech giant plans to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He indicates the company can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Sources indicate that should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

    Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the Upcoming World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

    It has been revealed that how many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

    If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

    Industry observers note that definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” says Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”.

    It has been revealed that it’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”.

    Recent findings suggest that one option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

    If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”.

    For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”.

    This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

    The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

    Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

    Sources indicate that composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

    Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they swiftly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”.

    It has been revealed that it’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

    Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

    If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

    According to recent reports, full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

    Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

    It has been revealed that A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Torres v. Carlson, at the moment pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

    Recent findings suggest that according to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada.".

    Industry observers note that assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

    It has been revealed that nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking problem with the district court's decisions to:.

    (1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;.

    (2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,.

    (3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

    As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

    Industry News: Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.
    • Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design.
    • The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

    What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

    The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

    Unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can promptly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland notes. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

    Industry observers note that vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception concern if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes notes.

    It has been revealed that broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

    According to recent reports, fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be new to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

    Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker indicates. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

    Recent findings suggest that while low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes states. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

    It has been revealed that A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

    According to recent reports, “There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty says. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

    It has been revealed that broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

    Recent findings suggest that while they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland claims. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

    Recent findings suggest that “A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland claims. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our fresh neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

    In a recent development, kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty states. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

Although prosecutors asked Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro for a five-year prison term, she imposed a suspended 24-month sentence and placed him on probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, over the government's objection.

    According to the government's evidence, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley in the 700 block of Taylor Street NW on May 11.

    Surveillance video showed him firing at a car parked in the alley. Seconds later, Drew fired toward a house near the alley in the 4100 block of Ninth Street NW, striking a boy who was playing basketball at a nearby recreation center. The boy suffered a leg injury.

    From the opinion in U.S. v. Drew, released Monday by D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer A. Di Toro:.

    According to recent reports, on August 10, 2026, Defendant Darius Drew entered a guilty plea to one count of Aggravated Assault and one count of Carrying a Pistol Without a License. Mr. Drew appeared before the Court for a sentencing hearing on November 13, 2026. At the hearing, the Court sentenced Mr. Drew to an aggregate term of incarceration of 24 months followed by 3 years of supervised release, with the execution of all but the 6 months he already served suspended in favor of 18 months of supervised probation.

    In addition to the standard conditions of probation, the Court required that Mr. Drew participate in a comprehensive mental health assessment and treatment as deemed necessary by the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency ("CSOSA"), undergo a substance abuse assessment and complete all treatment deemed necessary by CSOSA, and complete 90 hours of community service. He is required to register as a gun offender in the District of Columbia and remain registered for two years following the expiration of his period of probation. The Court entered an order requiring Mr. Drew to stay away from the location of the offense. During the period of probation, Mr. Drew is required to participate in either a GED program or vocational training and to maintain or seek employment. The Court also required Mr. Drew to appear before the Court for regularly-scheduled probation review hearings.

    In a recent development, because Mr. Drew was 19 years old at the time of this offense, he requested through counsel that he be sentenced under the Youth Rehabilitation Act ("YRA"), D.C. Code §§ 24-901 through 24-907. The Court now concerns this "written statement on the record of the reasons for its determination" that Mr. Drew is eligible for and will be sentenced under the YRA, D.C. Code §24-903(c)(l). In deciding to sentence Mr. Drew pursuant to the YRA, the Court considered all of the factors set forth in D.C. Code §24-903(c)(2). Specifically, the Court evaluated:.

    For the foregoing reasons, the Court concludes that Mr. Drew should be treated as a youth offender for the purpose of sentencing. Accordingly, the Court granted a sentence pursuant to the YRA in this case.

    Dirty windows or a streaky glass door are easy to notice and are easy to clean. Yet, cleaning windows and doors always seems like a chore we put off—even though it requires minimal work. No more excuses! You don’t need any fancy cleaners or tools when you can make this DIY glass cleaner recipe for free from supplies in your house.

    It has been revealed that save some dollars and keep things simple by mixing up your own DIY window cleaner with nothing more than a few pantry staples you likely have on hand. The following homemade window cleaner is a solution of ingredients that you can actually pronounce, like vinegar and water, and can whip up promptly and leave under your sink for the next time it’s needed. Here’s the recipe for success:.

    Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

    Before learning how to clean windows with vinegar, you’ll first want to gather the materials for this DIY glass cleaner. You’ll need distilled white vinegar (or lemon juice) and dish soap—a fragrant essential oil is nice to add, but not necessary.

    In this recipe, as with so many other nontoxic homemade cleaners, white vinegar plays a key role. Its acidity cuts through dirt and grease, an attribute that well equips the window cleaner to remove stuck-on debris and streaks.

    According to recent reports, if you’ve washed your windows for years with a commercial cleaner such as Formula 409 or even Windex, it’s likely that the glass sports a subtle, waxy film. That residue comes off easily with ordinary dish detergent, another ingredient contributing to the efficacy of homemade window cleaner.

    According to recent reports, in a spray bottle, combine ¼ cup of white vinegar with ½ teaspoon of liquid dish soap. Dilute the solution with 2 cups of water, then shake the bottle vigorously to mix the components. If you don’t have white vinegar on hand, you can substitute lemon juice. Like distilled white vinegar, lemon juice has a mild acidity that cuts through grease and grime with equal panache.

    Industry observers note that as a cleaning agent, there’s much to love about vinegar, but the strong odor isn’t everyone’s favorite thing. Fortunately, you can go a long way toward camouflaging the scent of your homemade glass cleaner by adding essential oil to the mixture in the spray bottle. Pick your favorite oil and add 10 to 15 drops.

    According to recent reports, with your homemade window cleaner now ready, spray the window glass with it. Then, using a lint-free cloth such as a microfiber cloth or chamois, wipe the cleaner across the entire surface you’re cleaning. The cleaner will dry fairly quickly, leaving behind a streak-free shine. For best results, follow up with a window squeegee, like the highly rated Mr. Siga window cleaning squeegee and scrubber.

    According to recent reports, this window-cleaning recipe works like a dream, but what do the individual components contribute to the mix? We’ll break it down for you.

    The main reason distilled white vinegar makes such a good glass cleaner is because it contains acetic acid. The colorless organic compound gives white vinegar its pungent flavor and odor, and kills some bacteria. When you wash windows with vinegar, not only will you be able to break down and remove dirt, grease, and mineral deposits, you’ll also be able to kill germs on hard surfaces around the home.

    It is vital to note, however, that vinegar-based cleaning solutions should not replace true sanitizing cleaners that remove 99.9 percent of disease-causing bacteria and viruses, the EPA standard for products labeled as sanitizers.

    Sources indicate that like white vinegar, the acid in lemon juice can effectively break down grime on windows and other glass surfaces. Citric acid in lemon juice is technically a bit stronger than vinegar’s acetic acid, though both are about equally effective when it comes to cleaning around the house.

    Several ingredients make up most liquid dish soaps on the market, but one ingredient in particular, sodium lauryl sulfate, gives dish soaps their impressive grease-busting abilities. The component bonds with oily particles and lifts them off of surfaces, which allows for easy removal when used with water.

    The best homemade window cleaner leaves behind an appealing scent. Many essential oils contain natural chemical components that are both cleansing and pleasantly scented. Tea tree essential oil, for example, doesn’t just smell great—it has antibacterial, antiseptic, and antifungal properties. Mixing it into your homemade window cleaner can help prevent mold and mildew growth, too.

    This set of 6 Lagunamoon essential oils includes orange, lavender and other aromas perfect for scenting cleaning solutions.

    As is the case when cleaning other parts of the home, water temperature makes a difference. Hot water has more kinetic energy than cold water, so it more easily agitates and lifts dirt particles off surfaces. While this may help with cleaning dishes and laundry to some extent, warm water isn’t essential for cleaning windows. Cold or tepid water will work, too.

    It has been revealed that A thorough window cleaning should be at the top of every homeowner’s seasonal cleaning to-do list. The start of spring when the weather warms is an opportune time to tackle this task both inside and outside your home. Before you start spritzing the glass, consider these useful window-cleaning tips:.

    Sources indicate that “Don’t forget to inspect your window hardware. If your finishes have dulled, you can apply a coat of beeswax to preserve and restore them. Also, it’s never a bad idea to take the time to put dry lubricant on the gears of your windows to keep all components functioning smoothly for seasons to come.”.

    —Michael Wandschneider, director of product management for Marvin.

    While you could use paper towels, a soft microfiber cloth works best for first removing dust and loose debris from windows. Use a separate clean microfiber cloth to work the homemade window cleaner along the glass surface and remove stubborn dirt and residue. Coffee filters are also handy for cleaning windows, as are squeegees. The latter are especially useful for deep-cleaning the outside of your windows, which you can DIY rather than paying for professional window cleaning.

    According to recent reports, the stainless-steel Unger Pro squeegee doesn’t leave streaks when cleaning glass, and can be used with an extended-reach pole. See the review.

    Using natural ingredients is eco-friendly and safer for your skin and lungs compared to the chemicals found in many commercial cleaners, but there are still a few safety considerations to be aware of when making your own window cleaner. Natural ingredients such as white vinegar, lemon juice, and essential oils are effective in homemade glass cleaners, but they do not replace true sanitizers that are proven to kill 99.9 percent of disease-causing pathogens.

    Recent findings suggest that the most crucial thing to remember when making window cleaner (or any other homemade cleaning solutions) is never to mix vinegar with chlorine bleach. When sodium hypochlorite, the basic chemical compound in bleach, mixes with the acetic acid found in vinegar, it gives off toxic chlorine gas. Chlorine gas can burn skin, cause shortness of breath, and can even be fatal with long-term exposure.

    Formulas for specialized commercial glass cleaners are often ammonia-based, and can leave streaks or foggy spots on some types glass. Car windows, for example, should not be cleaned with ammonia-based window cleaners because the residue poses a risk of obstructing the driver’s view. Natural glass cleaners that do not contain ammonia, such as the homemade window cleaner recipe above, don’t leave behind residue or streaks when wiped away using a clean microfiber cloth.

    Recent findings suggest that the best window cleaning solution is safe, natural, and effective. Following this recipe for a natural window cleaner can help you achieve all of these goals and leave you with clear, clean, and streak-free windows. Mixing in a few drops of essential oil adds a pleasant scent to the vinegar-based cleaner.

    Cleaning the windows in your home doesn’t have to be an overwhelming task. Consider focusing on one level or room at a time to keep the workload manageable. Remember, you should also clean the exterior windows and screens a few times a year.

    Yes, you can use rubbing alcohol to get windows clean if you don’t have vinegar on hand. To make the best window washing solution with rubbing alcohol, add 1½ cup water, 1½ cup rubbing alcohol, and 2 tablespoons of white vinegar (if you have any) to a spray bottle. Close the bottle, shake it to mix the ingredients, and use it to clean windows and other glass surfaces in your home.

    Ammonia-based commercial window cleaners leave behind a residue that can make windows look streaky. For streak free windows, try making your own natural homemade window cleaner using white distilled vinegar, water, lemon juice, essential oils, and dish soap.

    Start by cleaning the window tracks and frames with a solution of three parts white distilled vinegar and one part water. Then, combine white distilled vinegar, lemon juice, water, essential oils, and dish soap together and use the solution to clean the glass.

    • Sources indicate that if the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier.
    • In a recent development, however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger problem than just the outlet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Sources indicate that if the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier. Or maybe you need a new outlet in a bathroom, laundry room, or doggy wash station in your mudroom, which means you’ll need to install a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlet, required for any outlet within 6 feet of a water source. The good news is, wiring an outlet, whether standard or GFCI, is a project that you can do yourself, but you must take proper safety precautions.

    In a recent development, however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger problem than just the outlet. In these instances, it’s best to consult with a licensed electrician before you attempt to rewire it.

    Read through these steps for how to wire an outlet before you get started.

    While a capable homeowner can wire an outlet, it’s not a job for a reluctant or unsure DIYer. Start by assessing your comfort level, and call in a pro if you have doubts.

    According to recent reports, in many instances, you can wire an outlet from another outlet. In fact, if there’s an existing outlet in a room on the opposite side of the wall from where you’d like to add an outlet, the job can be pretty simple. In this situation, you can usually cut a newly introduced opening, install an electrical box, and add a new outlet without having to snake wires through studs. Use a stud finder to locate the studs on either side of the existing outlet and make sure to situate the new outlet within the same stud bay.

    Recent findings suggest that if you simply want more outlets in one location, it’s possible to replace an existing duplex outlet, which takes just two plugs, with a quad receptacle, which takes four. This can be helpful in a workshop or even in kitchens and bathrooms where two outlets just won’t cut it.

    It has been revealed that in either case, it’s vital that there’s enough capacity on the circuit to accommodate the additional draw. For 15-amp circuits, the maximum is usually eight outlets or lights. Any more receptacles than that might draw too much current for the breaker.

    According to recent reports, old-fashioned two-prong outlet connections aren’t grounded, which makes them dangerous in the event of an electrical fault. Without an electrician, it’s safe to convert a two-prong to a three-prong outlet only if the electrical box housing the outlet is metal and the cable feeding the box is armored. If these conditions are met, the box provides ground-fault protection (even though the outlet does not).

    Sources indicate that how can you tell, without opening the wall, if the electrical box meets the criteria? Simple: Use a voltage tester.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that from Doe v. Doe (E.D. Pa.), decided today by Judge Gerald Pappert:.

    Jane Doe alleges four X (formerly Twitter) users falsely accused her of having a sexual relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and doxxed her by posting on the social networking site her full name, employment and education history, phone numbers and addresses. Doe asserts claims for defamation, false light, public disclosure of private facts and aiding and abetting. She seeks to proceed under a pseudonym because she fears for her safety, along with additional reputational and professional harm. The Court denies the motion because Doe's fear of harm does not outweigh the public's interest in open litigation.

    In a recent development, [A.] Parties to a lawsuit typically must identify themselves. Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(a). In "exceptional cases," however, parties may proceed anonymously. To do so, "a plaintiff must show both (1) a fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable." Courts balance multiple factors in considering whether to let someone proceed anonymously, including (1) the extent the identity of the litigant has been kept confidential; (2) the bases upon which disclosure is feared or sought to be avoided; (3) the public interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the litigant's identity; (4) whether the matter is purely legal in nature; (5) whether the party seeking to sue anonymously has illegitimate motives; and (6) the universal level of public interest in access to the identities of the litigants. The purpose of this balancing test "is to allow a district court to determine whether a litigant has a reasonable fear of severe harm that outweighs the public's interest in open litigation." ….

    In a recent development, the first factor "does not support anonymity where the litigant's identity has never been confidential." Doe has not kept her identity confidential. After Defendants doxxed her, by posting her picture, phone numbers and prior addresses, she publicly responded by "den[ying] the connection to Epstein in the thread of Defendants' posts.".

    To establish fear of severe harm, Doe argues that "survivors and other named individuals have reported receiving death threats." Yet she does not allege how she will be threatened if forced to proceed under her real name, and courts reject "claims of harm or generalized fear that are found to be speculative and unsupported by evidence." As she notes, the Defendants have already shared her personal information with the public, so there is no greater risk if she proceeds under her own name.

    Doe also alleges a "risk of reputational and professional devastation." But "[c]ourts in this Circuit do not recognize purely social and reputational harms, without more, as valid bases to prevail on this factor." Embarrassment or economic harm is not enough to justify proceeding anonymously either. And because her identity was made public, "litigating publicly will afford Doe the opportunity to clear [her] name" and "will not contribute further to the harm that [she] alleges has already occurred.".

    According to recent reports, in assessing the public's interest, courts consider whether "other similarly situated litigants [would] be deterred from litigating claims." Doe provides no reason to believe similarly situated litigants would be deterred from bringing defamation claims due to fear of disclosing their identities. The Epstein-related cases she relies upon involve plaintiffs who Epstein sexually assaulted, not individuals falsely accused of having a relationship with him.

    If a plaintiff's claims are purely legal in nature, there is an "atypically weak public interest in knowing the litigant's identity." Doe's claims that Defendants falsely identified her as someone who had a sexual relationship with Epstein are inherently fact sensitive. For example, a key issue is whether Defendants "knew or were reckless about this falsity and had no good faith basis to claim that Plaintiff was the woman" identified in the Epstein files, and resolving that depends on the nature of the facts known to Defendants.

    There is no evidence that Doe has illegitimate motives to proceed anonymously, which favors anonymity. The universal level of public interest in access to the identities of litigants, however, always weighs in favor of disclosing a plaintiff's identity.

    The Court does not diminish the harm Doe claims to have suffered, but she has not established how using her real name would subject her to "severe harm," separate from what she has already allegedly endured from Defendants' past actions. Any harm she may suffer from using her own name is not outweighed by the "thumb on the scale that is the universal interest in favor of open judicial proceedings." ….

    Industry observers note that this is consistent, I think, with the cases generally holding that libel plaintiffs can't sue pseudonymously; see Roe v. Smith and the federal cases that it cites.

    Now that working from home has become commonplace, many of us are trying to create quiet environments in which we can complete our work without being distracted by noises from the next room or an overhead apartment.

    Whether you’re part of the growing gig economy and looking to soundproof your home office, your teen has rock star dreams, or your 8-year-old has started tap-dancing, you’ll find that a little soundproofing can go a long way toward keeping the peace and quiet at home.

    In a recent development, first, set reasonable expectations. Don’t expect an utterly silent room because you won’t get it. Room soundproofing techniques will reduce sound transfer from one room to another, but they won’t eliminate the loudest noises. Still, by employing the following methods, you can reduce distracting noise to a bearable level. These techniques can be used for any type of room—a home office, a nursery, or a family room, or to create a soundproof bedroom.

    Industry observers note that where possible, use the techniques in the adjacent rooms as well as the one you’re looking to soundproof. For example, if an attached garage that’s used as a workshop shares a common wall with the master bedroom, use soundproofing techniques on both the garage wall and the inside of the master bedroom wall for the best results. Learn how to soundproof a bedroom or other room to create a space where noises aren’t distracting.

    In a recent development, creating soundproof walls is most effective when done during construction, but there are several ways to put a damper on ambient and active noise after the fact to make a soundproof room. To minimize noise, consider the two strategies outlined here for how to soundproof a wall.

    Industry observers note that mass-loaded vinyl (MLV) is a sound-dampening product used everywhere from nightclubs and recording studios to hockey rinks, and it’s among the best soundproofing materials available. It comes on a roll and costs around $2 per square foot, depending on weight, length, and width. The thicker it is, the better it will be for blocking noise and ending echoes, but thickness, which can range from 1/16 inch to 1/4 inch, may not be listed in product specifications. It may instead be labeled by weight. Half-pound MLV weighs 1/2 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/16 inch thick; 1-pound MLV is 1 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/8 inch thick; 2-pound MLV is 1/4 inch thick.

    Industry observers note that while MLV can be hung directly on a wall, it performs best when sandwiched between drywall sheets. Doing so also allows you aesthetic options since the usually black, shiny MLV isn’t the most decoratively appealing surface. Keep in mind that MLV, such as Soundsulate, is heavy and awkward to work with. Hanging it is a two-person job, so be sure to enlist a helper.

    Tape measureMass-loaded vinylHeavy-duty scissors or utility knifeStep ladderDrywall nailsHammerType X drywall (optional).

    According to recent reports, prior to ordering MLV, carefully measure the walls you want to soundproof. Leaving gaps in MLV will drastically compromise its effectiveness, so you’ll want to buy enough for complete coverage from wall to wall and floor to ceiling. When calculating your needs, note that MLV tends to be sold on rolls of 2-foot or 4-foot widths.

    Industry observers note that measure a length of MLV that will reach floor to ceiling and then cut out a sheet with the scissors or utility knife. Cutting on top of scrap wood would be wise to protect your floor or work surface.

    Recent findings suggest that position the step ladder and put the MLV against the wall starting at either end, working to the other corner. To install it, snug it up against the ceiling, with your helper holding it in place. Using drywall nails and a hammer, attach the MLV to the upper portion of the wall at 12-inch intervals. Then attach the bottom portion at 12-inch intervals, and finally at 12- to 24-inch intervals down the sides of the sheet.

    Repeat Steps 2 and 3 as required until the entire wall is covered. For the best soundproof wall, butt the MLV right up against the preceding sheet so there are no gaps. You can overlap it for a potentially greater sound barrier, but you’ll have bumps and ridges if you do so. Overlapping is not recommended if you blueprint to paint, install wallpaper, or install additional drywall panels.

    Hang drywall on top of the MLV to make the soundproofing twice as effective and give you a surface for paint or other wall covering decor. Or read on for a quick solution to hiding the glossy black vinyl with curtains—a no-commitment decor project that will also enhance soundproofing. Sometimes called “soundproof drywall,” Type X drywall is 5/8 inch thick and fire rated, making it among the best options for noise dampening.

    According to recent reports, not for windows only, curtains can create drama on the walls of any room while offering considerable soundproofing benefits. They’re relatively inexpensive and as easy to remove as they are to install. While there are curtains specifically marketed as sound dampening or “acoustic,” blackout and thermal curtains, which are primarily sold to keep light out and warmth in, also provide noise reduction. Don’t let the term “blackout” fool you, though. These curtains come in many colors and styles—it’s the inner liner that provides the blackout/thermal effect. Even heavy fabrics like velvet provide some soundproofing.

    Keep in mind that when you double the weight of the fabric, its sound-reduction ability nearly triples. Yet more notable than weight is curtain construction; pleated curtains can be three times as effective against noise as those that hang straight.     Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

    Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches.     📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • According to recent reports, depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    While bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an concern you want to ignore. When a toilet bubbles, it indicates that negative air pressure (suction) is building up in the drain line, creating an airlock of sorts. Most likely this buildup of air is due to a clog.

    According to recent reports, depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative. Otherwise, you might have to call a plumber. Is a gurgling toilet dangerous? Not typically, but if the culprit is a broken or collapsed sewer line, it will have to be fixed, and the sooner the better. If the job is put off, waste could back up into toilets, showers, or tubs. The following guide will help you get to the root of toilet bubbling, and offer solutions to the problem.

    Clogs typically occur in one of two areas: somewhere in the drain system, which could be close to the toilet or farther down the main sewer line that connects to your community’s sewer system, or in your home’s vent stack (the pipe that allows sewer gasses to escape through the roof). To fix the gurgling toilet once and for all, you’ll need to identify the location of the clog and take steps to remove it.

    Ridgid’s Power Spin+ has an easy-to-use pull trigger and handle; can be attached to a power drill to dislodge serious blockages. Read the review.

    Addressing clogs is key to fixing air bubbles in your toilet—but not all clogs are created equal. A few troubleshooting steps can help you identify whether the solution is DIY-friendly, or if it’s time to call a plumber.

    It has been revealed that if the cause of the gurgling is in the drainpipe, simply plunging the toilet might create enough pressure to dislodge a light-to-moderate clog. Bathroom fixtures (tub, sink, shower) often connect to the same drain line that runs from the toilet, so you’ll want to seal off these drains with duct tape before plunging. If you plunge without sealing the drains, the pressure plunging creates can escape through other drain fixtures instead of dislodging the clog.

    Start by selecting the right plunger, such as the JS Jackson accordion-style plunger, which was a top pick in our researched guide to the best plungers. With the toilet bowl full of water, fit the head of the plunger tightly to the drain hole in the bottom of the bowl. Try to dislodge the clog with 10 to 15 firm pumping motions, then wait to see if the toilet gurgles again. If you don’t have a plunger handy, other ways of unclogging a toilet without one may be just as effective. However, if the gurgling continues, move on to the following steps.

    It has been revealed that A sewer snake (also known as a plumber’s snake or plumber’s auger) can often remove tough clogs in a drainpipe that plunging can’t manage. Featuring a long cable and a head with cutting blades for chopping through stubborn clogs, the best drain snakes may even have a manual or motorized crank.

    If you’re not sure how to snake a toilet, a manual toilet auger ($25 to $100 at home-improvement stores) is inserted into the toilet bowl. As you turn the crank, the head works its way down the drainpipe, cutting through clogs. This type of auger is limited to the distance of its cable reach, generally 5 to 15 feet.

    In a recent development, if a clog is so deep in the drainpipe that a small sewer snake cannot reach it, you can upgrade to a motorized auger that will reach 50+ feet, or rent a medium-sized drain cleaner from a home improvement store. Renting the equipment for an afternoon might run you $40 to $50, whereas calling a plumber to snake the drain could run you $150 to $300. Additional repairs, such as removing tree roots from a sewer line or fixing a broken sewer line, may be even costlier.

    Industry observers note that since the auger head on a motorized sewer snake is often too large to wind its way through the toilet bowl, the toilet should be removed from its base and the auger inserted into the drainpipe at floor level. When the machine is turned on, the auger will work its way down the line, its razor-sharp blades cutting through tough clogs.

    Industry observers note that for clogs even deeper in the sewer line—as far out as the middle of your yard—you’ll want to auger the lines from the sewer cleanout, which is just outside of your home, directly over the sewer pipe. To locate the cleanout, check your basement or crawlspace to see where the main sewer line exits your house. Many cleanout pipes extend a few inches above the ground and feature a large PVC cap, but others may terminate just below ground level. You may need to do a little digging to uncover it. Once you’ve removed the cap from the cleanout pipe with an adjustable wrench, auger the sewer line from there. If the toilet gurgling stops, you’ve successfully removed the sewer clog that caused it; if the sounds continue, try troubleshooting the vent stack.

    Sources indicate that checking and clearing the vent stack requires getting on the roof, so if you’re not completely comfortable with that, be safe and call the pros. Here’s how to check the vent stack yourself:.

    According to recent reports, vent clogs are often caused by leaves and debris, or even the carcass of a small animal that got stuck in the pipe. If the clog is within a few feet of the top of the pipe, you may be able to remove it with a straightened-out wire coat hanger or a toilet brush. Deeper clogs can often be removed by running water from a garden hose in the pipe, which can dislodge the clog, washing it down the pipe and out through the sewer.

    Recent findings suggest that can a gurgling toilet fix itself? Unfortunately, the answer is no. If the troubleshooting methods above failed to silence your gurgling toilet bowl, it’s time to call the plumber. Plumbers have specialized emergency plumbing tools and equipment, such as powerful sewer augers that can chop through anything blocking the main sewer line.

    According to Roto-Rooter, gurgling toilets can also indicate that tree roots have grown into the sewer line. If this is the case, repairs are best left to a professional plumber. Professionals can use mini cameras that drop into vent stacks to locate the source of the problem. There’s also a slim chance that the main sewer line in your yard has broken or collapsed, in which case excavation and professional repairs might be necessary.
