    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1698 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.
    • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
    • During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

    The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

    During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

    It has been revealed that the State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

    Sources indicate that the district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

    According to recent reports, we conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

    According to recent reports, the enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

    Industry observers note that through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

    Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

    In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and fresh parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

    Sources indicate that on May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

    1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

    H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

    Section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

    At problem here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

    Recent findings suggest that even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

    After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

    Industry observers note that the $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

    In a recent development, texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

    According to recent reports, I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a fresh requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

    Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

    Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

    I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

    Industry observers note that the petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the new Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

    More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S.
    • Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.
    • Sources indicate that “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” stated Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

    Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

    Sources indicate that “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” stated Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”.

    Sources indicate that “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”.

    “Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”.

    Sources indicate that “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”.

    According to recent reports, according to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

    In a recent development, much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

    In a recent development, during his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

    It has been revealed that specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

    According to recent reports, on some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”.

    According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

    According to recent reports, the FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

    In a recent development, the matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

    According to court records, Mercurio planned to incapacitate his father with a metal pipe and take his firearms to use in a mass casualty attack on Idaho churches in the name of ISIS. Mercurio also planned to use flame-covered weapons, explosives, knives, and a machete in the attacks. A search of his house revealed that he had butane canisters, lighters, a pair of handcuffs, a knife, and a machete, as well as several firearms belonging to his father. Days before the planned attack, Mercurio stood before an ISIS flag holding a knife and pledged his allegiance to ISIS. The FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before his planned attack. In addition to his plot to attack Idaho churches, in early 2023, he created an online repository for pro-ISIS content with the purpose of spreading the doctrine of the Islamic State.

    According to recent reports, “America’s founders wanted our Nation to be a place where the faithful of any denomination could exercise their religious beliefs freely and without fear of violence,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence demonstrates that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”.

    “The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” said U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. I commend the investigation by the FBI, as well as the valuable assistance provided by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.”.

    “With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”.

    The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.

    The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Heather S. Patricco and David G. Robins for the District of Idaho and Trial Attorney Matthew R. Hracho of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

    • An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.
    • According to recent reports, anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 12:52 pm CST.

    In a recent development, an Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock).

    An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

    According to recent reports, anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

    Sources indicate that court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

    According to recent reports, the officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

    According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”.

    Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

    Diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

    Our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

    Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

    Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

    Xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

    The Chief Customer Officer is a upcoming role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay. This is a customer-focused role in the most commercial sense: what a member earns from us, not the feature we shipped, is the centre of every decision.

    The measure of success is a Customer P&L that grows on what members hold and keep: LTV:CAC improving, approved-to-paid rising, churn falling, and customer contribution the business can plan against.

    Sources indicate that this is a banking role, not a requirements-gathering role, a marketing role, or a role you can run from a dashboard. Products are priced on the balance sheet and judged on the money they attract and keep.

    Sources indicate that this part matters as much as the mandate. The known failure mode for this role, in any company, is a CCO with a polished customer-insight deck and no ownership of the number. That is disqualifying here.

    Sources indicate that day 30: The Customer P&L baseline is documented across retail and institutional: customer contribution, LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, net paid-member growth, and assets attracted and kept. You have formed your own independent view of where members are won, lost, and under-served, and shared it with the CEO and Board.Day 60: The unified Customer operating model is live: one set of key results across Growth, Client Coverage, Mission PMs, and Product Design, read weekly from one source. Every mission PM owns a product's contribution and its price, and the roadmap is ranked on what it earns, built with Finance and the line leads.Day 90: At least one measurable improvement in LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, or net newly introduced AUM flow is live and attributable to a change you made, not a feature ship, an outcome moved. Every cell in your line has defined key results and an owner who explains the number every week.

    Impact Globally, Work Remotely.

    Shape the FutureImprove lives through cutting-edge technology, work 100% remotely from anywhere in the world.

    Great work-life balanceBuild amazing things with a balance of autonomy and collaborative teamwork. Set your own work schedule and make use of a flexible PTO strategy when you need to recharge.

    Sources indicate that expect ExcellenceCollaborate, learn, and grow with a high-performance team. Learn how you learn best - from books to conferences, you’ll get a yearly budget for your individual learning and development goals.

    At Xapo, we prioritize consumer protection and adhere to regulatory requirements by ensuring that all Xapiens are accountable for upholding principles of fair treatment, transparency, and ethical conduct in their interactions with customers and stakeholders.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

    It has been revealed that an eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

    “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”.

    According to recent reports, “This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

    “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” mentioned Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

    Sources indicate that “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of Upcoming York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

    According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

    Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of Newly introduced York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

    It has been revealed that al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in Newly introduced York. The picture below indicates al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

    Recent findings suggest that as alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

    The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

    Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

    In a recent development, on or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

    The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

    In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

    It has been revealed that on or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

    In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

    In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

    It has been revealed that on Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

    In a recent development, while in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    It has been revealed that for example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

    On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    Recent findings suggest that al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

    The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

    Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of Upcoming York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

    A superseding indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

    LexLab, the legal technology hub at the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, is launching a three-day artificial intelligence legal tool building course, Law & AI Certificate Lab.

    In a recent development, the intensive LAIC Lab course, offered Dec. 1-3, is a condensed, intensive version of one offered to law students over the course of a semester, offering lawyers and leaders a deep dive into the logic underlying legal AI while offering hands-on exploration of AI systems.

    The course allows students to work with AI company Legora and AI platform Harvey as well as Replit, an app and website builder.

    At the end of the certificate program, students should be able to move beyond using “chat” to build repeatable playbooks, checklists and other workflows; evaluate AI tools and vendors; determine whether tech should be bought or built; and manage privilege, confidentiality, conflicts and competence problems in AI-augmented practice.

    Tech Report: Court Concludes Allegation Against Rep. Max Miller Is "Substantially True" and Dismisses Defamation Claim

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I may not live in Ohio anymore, but there are some Ohio legal news stories I continue to follow.
    • Max Miller (R-OH) sued his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno), for defamation.
    • Miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I may not live in Ohio anymore, but there are some Ohio legal news stories I continue to follow. Here's one.

    Soon-to-be-former Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) sued his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno), for defamation. Now that suit has been dismissed, and arguably in the worst way for Miller: The court concluded that the core underlying allegation is "substantially true.".

    Miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident. As the court notes, an audio recording (that Miller released somehow thinking it would exonerate him) confirms the core of the claim. From the opinion:.

    Sources indicate that an audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno's contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring "bowling hot water on me." Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated "it was never done to hurt you with intent." Plaintiffs intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.

    Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is "categorically different" than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiffs burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

    The court also noted the lack of any evidence that Moreno was responsible for the Daily Mail's publication of the claims.

    Industry observers note that the court dismissed Miller's suit with prejudice and awarded costs and attorney fees. Additional litigation arising out of the Miller-Moreno divorce is pending, and it's always possible Miller will appeal. Moreno is not the first woman to accuse Miller of abuse.

    More background from the Washington Post here.

    [Note: As initially posted, I referred to Miller as "Former Rep. Miller." OF course, he is not yet a former representative, as his term has not yet ended, so I have updated the post accordingly.

    The First Amendment, University Investigations, and Anti-Israel Lawprof's Case Against Univ. of Kentucky

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D.
    • This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….
    • Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto:.

    This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….

    Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.

    Sources indicate that but the order set an evidentiary hearing two weeks later to address these fact-dependent questions and Woodcock's request for a preliminary injunction. The investigation—which had lasted more than a year and whose report was already overdue—could not "last forever" without threatening Woodcock's First Amendment rights. And the University of Kentucky's corresponding "reassignment" of Woodcock from teaching duties throughout the investigation was increasingly hard to justify, particularly given the absence of any articulated suspicion of classroom disruption….

    Industry observers note that then, one week after the TRO decision, the outside investigator's 134-page sealed (for now) report finally landed. {That report is provisionally under seal pending the resolution of a motion to seal, which will be referred to a Magistrate Judge.} ….

    [Now], the Dean of the law school could decide whether to lift Woodcock's reassignment from teaching and restore him to the classroom for the spring semester. This could happen as late as mid-December, according to counsel, without prejudicing Woodcock's ability to teach…. [And] the University President could decide, based on the investigative report, whether (in his view) Woodcock violated any laws or policies….

    It has been revealed that the report and Woodcock's response have been published by the Kentucky Lantern (McKenna Horsley); Woodcock reports that this is because they were publicly filed in a parallel state case. The court had this to say about Woodcock's request for a temporary injunction to block any findings by the University President:.

    During previous hearings, this Court observed that Woodcock's effort to end his reassignment from teaching stood on firmer ground that his request to halt the investigation itself. That view rested largely on caselaw that contemplated speech-related investigations consistent with the First Amendment yet considered whether any attendant consequences of such investigations abridged those rights based on a retaliatory purpose, chilled speech, or both. {See generally, e.g., Sensabaugh v. Halliburton (6th Cir. 2019) (no adverse action based on "letter of guidance" and reprimand in the context of a "independent law firm" investigation involving "scores of documents and text messages" and "seventeen different witnesses"); Moore v. Garnand (9th Cir. 2023) ("[W]e never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment, as our holding rested on much more than just a retaliatory investigation[.]").} ….

    Woodcock insists that the First Amendment bars the President from spending "weeks poring over documents" unrelated to "any arguable policy violation." "Whatever the University decides about spring teaching, findings issued on the investigator's report would injure Woodcock irreparably on their own." To the extent that review entails an inquiry into his political beliefs, Woodcock contends, the process is illegitimate and should be enjoined immediately….

    Industry observers note that [But] a substantial body of caselaw indicates that a speech-related investigation alone generally doesn't amount to retaliation or adverse action. {See, e.g., Churchill v. Univ. of Colorado at Boulder (Colo. App. 2010) ("Courts have concluded that investigations alone are not adverse employment actions."); Sensabaugh (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding no adverse action even when context included a "painstakin[g] investigation"); Couch v. Board. of Trustees of Memorial Hospital of Carbon County (10th Cir. 2009) (investigation didn't amount to adverse action supporting First Amendment retaliation); Benningfield v. City of Houston (5th Cir. 1998) ("Although a reprimand can constitute an adverse employment action, an investigation does not[.]"); Moore ("[W]e have never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment"); Bell v. Sheriff of Broward County 1375 (11th Cir. 2021) ("[D]eputy Bell's five-day suspension with pay pending an investigation into his conduct is not an adverse action."). But as emphasized in the Court's previous TRO opinion, the caselaw in this area is hardly uniform and uncertainty remains about how different circuits might approach each specific factual scenario. See, e.g., Holt v. Pennsylvania (3d Cir. 2017) ("Our Circuit has not considered whether the initiation of an internal investigation can constitute an 'adverse action' for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim, and our sister circuits are split on the glitch.").} The collateral consequences of an investigation, by contrast, may create an intolerable chill that could warrant judicial intervention. See, e.g., Levin v. Harleston (2d Cir. 1992); White v. Lee (9th Cir. 2000). The First Amendment leaves at least some room for employers to investigate their employees for perceived misconduct, even when the alleged offenses relate to speech. Waters v. Churchill (1994) (plurality op.) ("Only [investigative] procedures outside the range" of reasonableness violate First Amendment despite investigation's "risk of erroneously punishing protected speech."); Gartenberg v. Cooper Union (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (even protected speech may be relevant to determining "whether actionable harassment occurred").

    In a recent development, woodcock hasn't pointed to any precedent halting a school's investigation based only on its existence or the "brand" or "reputational harm" that it might produce. To the contrary, the two precedents on which he relies most heavily are easily distinguishable.

    In a recent development, sweezy v. New Hampshire (1957), is a 70-year-old precedent concerning a state attorney general's investigation into a professor's affiliation with the Communist and Progressive Parties. It had little, if anything, to say about the operations, autonomy, or academic interests of a university. Contra, e.g., Regents of University of Michigan v. Ewing (1985).

    According to recent reports, fischer v. Thomas (6th Cir. 2022), likewise sits far afield from the context of university governance and academic speech. In that pre-enforcement challenge, the Sixth Circuit barred a state judicial commission from initiating formal proceedings against two judicial candidates after it "sen[t] vague and threatening letter to [the] candidates on the eve of election." The opinion didn't address whether an investigation or its concluding findings amounted to adverse action or retaliation….

    Sources indicate that fifth, even assuming Woodcock could establish a likelihood of success on the merits of his retaliation claim, to obtain a TRO he'd have to show irreparable harm and the balance of the equities relative to third parties and the public. Irreparable harm likely requires at least some showing of subjective chill as well; otherwise a court would be left to wonder why and "whether it needs to act now." ….

    It has been revealed that the current record does precious little to "identify speech that [Woodcock] wishes to make in the future but for the threat of prosecution of that future speech." Despite boilerplate assertions that he'd otherwise say and write more about Israel and Palestine, it's hardly clear that this investigation has chilled Woodcock's speech at all. He points to a paper called "A Law and Economics Argument for Ending Israel" that he hasn't yet submitted to the law reviews; diminished posting on his blog, called "the Antizionist Legal Studies Movement;" and allegedly decreased Twitter activity. Yet Woodcock's social-media and listserv posting hasn't stopped altogether; during this investigation he has continued to post on X and the AALS online discussion groups, including about Israel; he has filed at least four lawsuits, several of which have been covered in the press; he maintains a webpage supplying information about and soliciting support for his speech and litigation. Without further evidence, the Court cannot conclude that Woodcock will be chilled over the next two weeks.

    Although the general tendency in the caselaw to treat First Amendment violations as irreparable harm cautions against assigning dispositive weight to this factor, the weakness of Woodcock's showing on the current record at least cuts against automatic or presumptive injunctive relief to ameliorate any purported self-censorship….

    The court also pointed to the university's own interest in speaking about Woodcock's speech:.

    [A]n injunction barring the President from reacting to the investigator's findings would—even on Woodcock's own terms—remedy one arguable free-speech violation with another. As any law professor knows, Justice Brandeis taught that the "remedy" for disfavored speech should ordinarily be more speech—not additional suppression. A college president, just like a law professor, may presumptively speak—privately or publicly—about a matter of public and professional interest such as this. Indeed, both have done so during this process.

    And President Capiluto's own speech rights aren't the only countervailing interests at glitch. The University has its own governance interests in the orderly and prompt resolution of a high-profile pending investigation. See Ewing ("Academic freedom thrives not only on the independent and uninhibited exchange of ideas among teachers and students, … but also, and somewhat inconsistently, on autonomous decisionmaking by the academy itself."). "Without this ability to investigate, a public employer would be left without recourse and would lose its 'greater leeway in its dealings with citizen employees.'".

    Given these compounding considerations, the Court concluded that no temporary order revisiting the Court's prior orders and specifically restraining the President was warranted based on these allegations of objective chill (regarding Woodcock's likelihood of success on the merits), subjective chill (regarding any irreparable harm associated with Woodcock's speech pending the forthcoming presidential findings), or the public and third-party interest in an orderly and prompt conclusion to an academic investigation….

    Industry observers note that this order, to be clear, does not resolve whether the University officials' past actions constituted retaliation in violation of the First Amendment—a distinct and retrospective question, for which damages and attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 & 1988 are at least potentially available (though the Defendants of course disagree). While those historical facts are necessary to Woodcock's showing of likelihood of success on the merits, even if proved they are not sufficient to warrant a restraining order, which requires a showing of ongoing chilled speech.

    It has been revealed that nor does this order address the propriety of any discipline that Woodcock might eventually face. As described above, those questions haven't ripened and follow their own administrative process—one the Sixth Circuit specifically contemplated might alter the abstention analysis….

    In a recent development, there will still be a preliminary injunction hearing on Dec. 3, and for it the court orders extra briefing on the following "disputed factual problems":.

    Lattarulo’s lawsuit alleges that agents targeted him because of his advocacy and seized information that included confidential communications with his clients.

    Burroughs’ ruling mandates that federal officials preserve all copied cellphone data without accessing it as litigation continues, according to a story by Law.com.

    A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

    Federal prosecutors in Newly introduced York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

    It has been revealed that according to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of Fresh York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

    The order also shows that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

    Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

    In a recent development, balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

    Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 11:01 am CST.

    California Gov. Gavin Newsom looks on during a bill-signing event Aug. 21, 2025, in Sacramento, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

    In a recent development, district attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s strategy to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

    In a recent development, the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which represents the plaintiffs, argued Monday that the governor was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting 548 death penalty sentences. The plaintiffs also challenged Newsom’s broad death penalty commutations without considering individual circumstances, beyond whether a person has more than one felony conviction. Existing law permits crime victims the opportunity to speak before a governor can commute someone.

    “Gov. Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” the plaintiffs said. “He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

    It has been revealed that newsom revealed Nov. 5 the commutations of all people on death row to life in prison without parole. The governor wrote a letter that remarked state-sanctioned killing undermines the legal system’s foundation and counters California’s values.

    Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

    Newsom moves to commute 548 death sentences, emptying California’s death row.

    #55652. 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1077 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that you expect danger in the city.
    • There’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • Recent findings suggest that I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that you expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    There’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    Recent findings suggest that I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Industry observers note that notable note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    Cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    Sources indicate that ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    #55650. Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    Sources indicate that did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    It has been revealed that hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. New York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    According to recent reports, the story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. Newly introduced Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    It has been revealed that in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    Sources indicate that we’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    In fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest revealed, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    According to recent reports, the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    But that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    How long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Fresh American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    Chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Upcoming American Wilderness.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 12:39 pm CST.

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing during closing statements in the ongoing 11-week trial involving trade secrets theft and sanctions evasion that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes.

    In a recent development, according to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, told jurors that Huawei spent two decades pursuing growth “by any means possible.”.

    To illustrate the trade secrets allegations, Arfa played a video of a former Huawei employee removing part of Tappy, T-Mobile’s robot for testing phone touchscreens, from the carrier’s lab. She also revealed side-by-side images of Cisco’s and Huawei’s router source code, saying the two matched exactly—down to an engineer’s stray comment mentioning someone named “Bob.”.

    “This simply couldn’t happen without copying,” Arfa said in her summation.

    She further alleged that Huawei managers encouraged theft by paying bonuses for obtaining confidential competitor information, and that employees boasted about it on an internal forum.

    On the sanctions compliance allegations, prosecutors said Huawei secretly controlled Skycom, a subsidiary that supplied sensitive technology to Iran’s government. Arfa said the organization repeatedly lied about owning Skycom. She also pointed to admissions by Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer, who signed a deferred prosecution agreement after spending three years under house arrest. Meng acknowledged that Skycom’s operations violated U.S. sanctions, and that she misled HSBC, Huawei’s primary bank, about its compliance, Arfa noted.

    Huawei, one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world, denies the allegations, contending that the case rests on the independent actions of rogue employees who were disciplined.

    The government revealed the case in 2019. The company is represented by Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe.
